2. Literature Review and Theoretical Framework

Three streams of financial economic literature shape our analysis of how open-source AI releases
transmit shocks through the stock markets. First, research on asymmetric volatility dynamics
shows how sector-specific stress impacts options-implied spreads. Next, behavioral finance
highlights the role of crashophobia and tail-risk hedging in elevating tech-sector fear. Finally, the
economics of open-source AI access explains how proprietary moats erode when high-
performance alternatives become freely available. We bring these concepts together to build an
empirical framework and interpret our findings..

2.1 Asymmetric Volatility Dynamics and Implied Fear Spreads

Financial theory establishes that equity volatility reacts asymmetrically to market returns, a
dynamic usually attributed to leverage effects and volatility feedback mechanisms (Black, 1976;
Christie, 1982). When asset values decline, equity leverage expands mechanically, which pushes
up risk and drives demand for downside protection. Within options markets, this asymmetry
shows up in the steepness of the option volatility skew and the relative pricing of index-level
implied volatility (Bakshi et al., 2003).

Broad market indices like the S&P 500 reflect diversified macroeconomic conditions, captured
by the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX). Sector-specific indices, by contrast, capture concentrated
structural exposures. The Nasdaq-100 Volatility Index (VXN) isolates the expected volatility of
major technology and growth equities. When the VXN/VIX ratio expands significantly, options

This interpretation aligns with the established view that the VIX captures broad market fear

structural stress rather than systemic risk (Dennis & Mayhew, 2002).

This distinction is central to our study. A widening VXN/VIX spread signals that markets view
open-source AI as a sector-specific threat to technology firms' future profit margins. A
compressed or flat spread, on the other hand, would suggest that investors see these releases as a
broad macroeconomic risk. We therefore rely on the VXN/VIX spread as our primary measure of
tech-sector fear.

2.2 Behavioral Heuristics and Crashophobia

The asset pricing literature highlights the role of investor sentiment and behavioral heuristics in
options pricing. Unlike rational expectations models, which assume investors form unbiased
probability assessments, behavioral finance recognizes that subjective fears and cognitive biases
systematically distort options prices (Barberis & Thaler, 2003).

Bates (2000) formalized the concept of crashophobia, demonstrating that out-of-the-money put
options systematically trade at rich valuations because institutional investors maintain persistent
subjective fears of sudden, discontinuous market drops. This demand for tail-risk protection
persists even when objective probabilities of extreme events remain low, reflecting a behavioral
bias rather than rational risk assessment.

The demand for such crash protection has been shown to affect option prices directly. Bollen and
Whaley (2004) show that implied volatility changes are driven by net buying pressure, with
index put options exerting the strongest influence on S&P 500 option volatility. This empirical
evidence supports the crashophobia framework by demonstrating that institutional demand for
put options drives up implied volatility.

In high-beta technology portfolios, this effect is amplified during periods of paradigm shifts.
When incumbents face credible disruption, as with the emergence of open-weight frontier AI
models, the subjective probability of a sudden valuation collapse increases. This heightened fear
manifests in options markets through increased demand for out-of-the-money puts on technology
equities, contributing to the widening VXN/VIX spread we expect to observe.

This framework provides a behavioral explanation for our empirical findings. If institutional

                                    42.3 Modern AI Economics, Diffusion, and Intangible Valuation Spillovers

Recent financial economic literature increasingly focuses on how generative artificial
intelligence and open-source diffusion reshape firm-level valuations, capital expenditure
strategies, and technological spillovers. Unlike traditional information technology investments
that scale gradually through standard capital accumulation channels, generative AI functions as a
general purpose technology characterized by rapid, highly synchronized diffusion (Chen, Shi, &
Srinivasan, 2024; Brookings, 2025).

Empirical work examining corporate responses to AI innovations highlights a crucial tension
between proprietary moat protection and open-source accessibility. While early studies
documented positive equity valuation effects for firms adopting closed-source generative
systems, subsequent research demonstrates that the introduction of high-performance open-
weight models fundamentally alters this calculus. The Linux Foundation (2025) reports that
commercial open-source startups average seven times greater valuations at IPO compared to
closed-source peers. This finding suggests that markets reward open-source business models
while simultaneously penalizing incumbent proprietary firms facing disruption.

Open-source releases lower adoption costs and reduce concerns about proprietary data lock-in,
which in turn cuts into the expected profit margins of incumbent software providers. Event study
evidence from Yang (2026) reveals an average cumulative abnormal return of 0.37%, equivalent
to $7.4 million in value creation, for public companies releasing open-source innovations. This
positive reaction increases with the company's proprietary innovation, suggesting that markets
view open-source as complementary to proprietary strategies when firms can capture value
through appropriability regimes.

Consequently, capital markets are forced to reprice enterprise value and terminal cash flow
expectations; particularly across intangible assets, which now account for approximately 90% of
S&P 500 value, up from 17% in 1975 (Andersen Global, 2026). As AI systems both consume
and produce these intangibles in a continuous value-creation loop, options markets capture this
structural repricing far faster than backward-looking accounting metrics. Institutional risk
managers, seeking tail-risk protection against potential model disruption, drive this concentrated
demand for out-of-the-money puts. This, in turn, inflates implied volatility surfaces and positions
options-implied fear spreads as leading indicators of long-term asset impairment well before
fundamental earnings revisions materialize.

2.4 Disruption of Proprietary Software Moats and Capital Expenditure Cycles

The economic valuation of software and AI firms relies heavily on the maintenance of
proprietary economic moats, network effects, and high switching costs (Arthur, 1989; Shapiro &
Varian, 1999). Industrial organization theory establishes that firms with strong barriers to entry
can sustain above-normal profits over extended periods (Tirole, 1988). Traditional enterprise

premium valuations supported by these exact advantages.

The rapid proliferation of open-weight frontier models from Chinese labs challenges these
traditional valuation frameworks. Economic analysis of open-source software diffusion indicates
that high-performance open-weight alternatives compress proprietary economic rents by
commoditizing foundational layers of technology (von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003). As high-
performance models from DeepSeek, Zhipu AI, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI become widely
available without expensive licensing fees, market participants must reprice the terminal growth
rates and capital expenditure returns of incumbent technology leaders. This study contributes to
the literature by providing the first empirical examination of how options markets price
successive open-source AI release shocks.

To evaluate how financial markets transmit structural shocks from open-source artificial

Abstract:
This paper argues that market governance mechanisms should be considered a key approach in the governance of artificial intelligence (AI), alongside traditional regulatory frameworks. While current governance approaches have predominantly focused on regulation, we contend that market-based mechanisms offer effective incentives for responsible AI development. We examine four emerging vectors of market governance: insurance, auditing, procurement, and due diligence, demonstrating how these mechanisms can affirm the relationship between AI risk and financial risk while addressing capital allocation inefficiencies. While we do not claim that market forces alone can adequately protect societal interests, we maintain that standardised AI disclosures and market mechanisms can create powerful incentives for safe and responsible AI development. This paper urges regulators, economists, and machine learning researchers to investigate and implement market-based approaches to AI governance.

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Metric / outcome | COSS evidence | Proprietary-software comparator | Investor interpretation | Source and limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue growth | Red Hat reported FY2019 revenue of **$3.4B, up 15% YoY**, immediately before IBM’s acquisition. No retrieved study estimates a representative COSS growth rate or matched COSS–proprietary difference. (pqac-00000017) | No matched proprietary-company growth statistic was reported in the retrieved evidence. | A prominent COSS firm achieved solid growth, but one successful acquired company cannot establish a COSS growth premium. | Batista (2026) is a broad analytical review, not a matched-company panel or causal financial study; the Red Hat figure is company-specific and subject to survivor selection. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000017) |
| Gross margin | No reliable COSS-versus-proprietary gross-margin comparison was found. COSS support, consulting and adaptation models can be labor-intensive, whereas standardized assurance and managed SaaS have greater scale economies and low marginal subscriber costs. (pqac-00000034) | Proprietary SaaS also benefits from low software-distribution costs, but no matched gross-margin estimate was available. | “Open source” alone does not determine gross margin; revenue mix matters. Services-heavy COSS should generally have structurally lower gross margins than hosted SaaS or proprietary licenses, but the retrieved literature does not quantify the gap. | Fermigier (2026) explicitly says its treatment is conceptual and states no empirical magnitudes; its propositions are model-conditional and await population data. (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038) |
| Operating margin / profitability | No representative COSS operating-margin comparison was found. The evidence emphasizes that free users, community maintenance, hosted infrastructure and enterprise sales still carry costs; relicensing has **not clearly been shown to improve vendor financial results**. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012) | No matched proprietary operating-margin benchmark was reported. Proprietary models possess stronger direct appropriability but may incur conventional R&D and sales costs. | Claims that community development automatically produces superior profitability are unsupported. Value creation by the project can greatly exceed value captured by the sponsoring company. | Foster (2024) studies three relicensing/fork cases, not accounting margins; Batista’s review documents structural underinvestment and free-riding rather than firm-level profitability. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019) |
| Free-to-paid conversion | No defensible COSS-specific conversion benchmark was found. General freemium SaaS evidence suggests **2%–5%** is typical; one anonymized B2B SaaS case improved from **3.8% to 7.4%** after product-led optimization. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045) | The available figures are generic freemium SaaS—not an open-source/proprietary comparison. | A large free community is not equivalent to monetizable demand. Low conversion can make paying customers subsidize a large free population; open-core firms must withhold enough differentiated value without making the community edition unattractive. | The 2%–5% figures come from freemium literature of uncertain representativeness. CloudMetrics is one anonymized case and cannot establish a COSS advantage; definitions and observation windows vary. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048) |
| Net revenue retention (NRR) | No COSS-specific NRR benchmark was found. In the anonymized CloudMetrics case, freemium-acquired customers reached **127% NRR**, versus **109%** for sales-led customers; team-workspace adopters reached **142%**, versus **114%** for non-adopters. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045) | General top-quartile SaaS NRR is reported as **above 120%**; this is not an open-source control group. (pqac-00000046) | Product-led acquisition can yield high expansion revenue, but the available evidence does not show that openness—not product design, collaboration effects or cohort selection—caused superior NRR. | One anonymized company, minimal citation history and no random assignment between acquisition models; it is evidence about freemium, not COSS as a licensing model. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045) |
| Private valuations and financing | In a selected sample of **44 visible open-source developer tools, 2020–2025**, Open Core + SaaS companies had **$40M median funding** and a top quartile above **$185M**; reported valuations included Supabase **$5B**, Grafana **$6B**, Vercel **$9.3B**, Hasura/PlanetScale/Sentry **$1B each**. Hosted-SaaS median funding was **$30M**. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029) | No matched proprietary cohort or risk-adjusted valuation multiple was analyzed. A 2025 Linux Foundation-associated claim—quoted secondhand—says COSS startups averaged **7×** closed-source peers’ IPO valuations. (pqac-00000040) | COSS can attract very large valuations when paired with managed services and enterprise monetization, but the evidence does not establish that openness causes a valuation premium. | Pandey’s sample was purposive and intentionally included about **15 unicorn/major-acquisition successes**; private valuations were sometimes estimated, failures were underrepresented, and no multivariate controls were used. The extraordinary 7× claim is not independently validated in the retrieved material. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000032) |
| Valuation multiples | No reliable matched EV/revenue or price/sales comparison was found. Headline company valuations and acquisition prices are available, but not standardized multiples measured at common dates. | No comparable proprietary multiples were supplied. | Investors should not infer a COSS multiple premium from absolute valuations; growth, revenue quality, market cycle, company age and cloud mix must be controlled. | The Linux Foundation / Serena / COSSA-style evidence is exposed to definitional discretion, survivor bias and promoter conflicts: a foundation hosting projects, an open-source-focused investor and a trade association all benefit from favorable COSS conclusions. The retrieved evidence supplies no auditable matched sample supporting the 7× figure. (pqac-00000040) |
| Post-IPO stock performance | No systematic study of COSS post-IPO total returns versus proprietary software was found. HashiCorp went public at an approximately **$14B valuation** in 2021 and was acquired for **$6.4B** in 2025—about **54% below** that IPO valuation, although this is not a shareholder total-return calculation. (pqac-00000025) | No matched proprietary IPO return series was available. Separately, an event study of five open-weight AI releases found proprietary/high-beta technology stocks returned **−0.63% abnormally** on the Kimi K3 announcement day, **−1.08% over days 0–5**, and **−0.81% over days 0–10**. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042) | The HashiCorp outcome cuts against treating a successful COSS IPO as proof of durable public-market value. Open-source competition can also reduce proprietary incumbents’ expected rents. | IPO valuation versus acquisition enterprise value is not the same as an investor return and ignores issuance, dilution and interim price paths. Krause’s event study covers only five 2025–2026 AI events and exposed technology stocks, not a COSS-versus-proprietary IPO cohort. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041) |
| Acquisition prices relative to IPO prices | HashiCorp: **$14B IPO valuation → $6.4B IBM acquisition**, approximately **0.46×** the IPO valuation. Red Hat: IBM paid **$34B** in 2019; no comparable IPO-price ratio is supplied. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000025) | No systematic proprietary-company acquisition-to-IPO ratio was reported. | COSS can produce large strategic exits, but HashiCorp demonstrates that a multibillion-dollar sale can still crystallize substantial value compression from an IPO benchmark. | Headline transaction values do not measure VC or public-shareholder returns without invested capital, dilution, holding periods, debt and distributions. Red Hat and HashiCorp are exceptional survivors. |
| Major acquisitions | IBM–Red Hat **$34B** (2019), Microsoft–GitHub **$7.5B** (2018), and IBM–HashiCorp **$6.4B** (2025) illustrate strategic demand for open-source ecosystems, enterprise customers and developer distribution. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000033) | Salesforce–Slack **$27.7B** is cited as open-source-adjacent rather than clean COSS evidence; classifications are inherently contestable. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000033) | Large exits prove that some COSS assets are valuable, not that the average COSS investment outperforms proprietary software. Acquirers often buy the commercial wrapper, customer base and service layer—not freely available code alone. | Illustrative transactions, not a census. GitHub and Slack do not fit a narrow single-vendor COSS definition, making category choices capable of materially changing reported outcomes. |
| VC exit outcomes | A 2006 VentureXpert search identified **135 US VC-backed firms** mentioning “Linux,” “Apache” or “open source,” versus nearly **8,000** VC-backed software/Internet firms during 1998–Aug. 2006; many of the 135 were not directly commercializing OSS. (pqac-00000031) | The roughly 8,000-company software/Internet universe is not a matched proprietary control group, and exit returns were not calculated. | Historically, COSS was a small and heterogeneous fraction of venture software. Modern success stories do not by themselves establish superior fund-level returns. | Mann’s keyword screen is broad, old and prone to classification error; it reports financing incidence rather than IRR, MOIC or exit probabilities. (pqac-00000031) |
| Failures, shutdowns and non-exits | No credible population failure or shutdown rate was found. Pandey classified firms as active, acquired, public or shut down, but selected visible projects, excluded projects dormant before 2023 and acknowledged that failed commercialization attempts were underrepresented. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000032) | No matched proprietary failure rate was reported. | This missing denominator is decisive: success-only acquisition and IPO statistics cannot support an expected-return conclusion for a prospective VC or public-equity investor. | Severe survivorship and left-truncation bias. Studies of OSS disproportionately examine successful, well-maintained projects, while abandoned projects fail quietly. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000027) |
| Cloud free-riding and rent capture | Hyperscalers can commercialize managed services based on OSS while original vendors bear development costs. AWS’s Elasticsearch offering helped prompt Elastic’s 2021 relicensing; AWS then forked Elasticsearch 7.10.2 as OpenSearch. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000010) | Proprietary vendors can legally exclude imitators and retain more direct control over licensing rents. | Open distribution may accelerate adoption but weaken appropriability. The party controlling hosting, distribution and customer relationships may capture more value than the project originator. | Evidence is strong on mechanisms and documented cases but weak on quantified effects on revenue, margin or shareholder return. Elastic employees already supplied over **95%** of Elasticsearch code changes, challenging claims that broad outside development necessarily lowers vendor R&D costs. (pqac-00000010) |
| Open-core cannibalization and relicensing/forks | Giving away too much can reduce upgrade incentives; restricting too much can damage adoption. Relicensing produced Elasticsearch→OpenSearch, Terraform→OpenTofu and Redis→Valkey; resulting foundation forks generally had greater organizational diversity, while financial gains to the original vendors remain unproven. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012) | Proprietary firms avoid a legally protected community fork but sacrifice the low-friction distribution, trust and external innovation associated with openness. | The right to fork limits the durability of a COSS vendor’s moat. A license change may protect near-term monetization yet create a competing substitute and destroy community goodwill. | Foster’s three-case organizational study does not estimate causal financial effects, and the forks were still young. Fermigier’s result—that fork capability shrinks the incentive to enclose—is a formal comparative-static result, not measured company performance. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037) |


*Table: A metric-by-metric comparison of what the evidence does—and does not—show about COSS versus proprietary software. The table distinguishes company examples and generic SaaS benchmarks from representative comparative studies, while highlighting survivor bias, missing failure denominators and industry-report conflicts.*

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing

        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The valuation of publicly traded software-as-a-service firms depends on how revenue expansion translates into profitability and enterprise value, making the growth–profitability trade-off important for corporate finance, investment analysis, and market valuation. Existing research offers limited evidence on whether the Rule of 40 has the same valuation relevance across development stages when its growth and profitability components are examined separately. This study assesses how revenue growth and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization margin, independently and jointly, are associated with annual enterprise value growth across revenue-defined groups and whether the Rule of 40 provides a consistent valuation-related indicator. The analysis uses a balanced panel of 30 software-as-a-service companies publicly traded on the United States capital market, with source data covering 2018–2024 and 180 firm-year observations analyzed for 2019–2024; firms are assigned to three fixed groups according to 2018 revenue. The empirical design combines Pearson correlations, pooled and group-specific linear regressions, interaction modelling, median-based growth–profitability profiling, Rule-of-40 quartiles, a binary comparison based on the conventional 40-point benchmark, and 1st/99th percentile winsorization of enterprise value growth. Firm-clustered standard errors with finite-sample correction are used for the principal full-sample regressions. Revenue growth showed a positive descriptive correlation with enterprise value growth (r = 0.165) and was statistically significant in the baseline firm-clustered regression (β = 0.847, SE = 0.295, p = 0.008; R² = 0.027; adjusted R² = 0.022), after adding EBITDA margin (β = 0.837, p = 0.013), and in the interaction specification (β = 0.791, p = 0.014). EBITDA margin (β = −0.043, p = 0.783), the revenue-growth–EBITDA interaction (β = −0.011, p = 0.287), and the stand-alone Rule of 40 (β = 0.154, p = 0.428) were insignificant. Formal pooled interaction tests did not identify significant cross-group slope differences for revenue growth (F(2, 29) = 1.281, p = 0.293), EBITDA margin (F(2, 29) = 0.251, p = 0.780), or the Rule of 40 (F(2, 29) = 1.325, p = 0.282). Among lower-revenue firms, high growth combined with a high margin was associated with median enterprise value growth of 28.8%, versus 15.9% for high growth with a low margin and −7.0% for low growth with a low margin; in the full sample, the third Rule-of-40 quartile recorded the highest median enterprise value growth of 31.6%, compared with 18.4% in the highest quartile. A direct comparison of observations with the Rule of 40 ≥ 40 versus < 40 produced no significant valuation difference (β = −4.445, p = 0.424). These findings indicate that revenue growth has the clearest contemporaneous association with enterprise-value dynamics, whereas the Rule of 40 is better interpreted as a contextual descriptive indicator than as a universal valuation threshold.</jats:p>

Abstract:
PurposeThe United States (US) sugar program protects domestic sugar farmers from unrestricted imports of heavily-subsidized global sugar. Sugar-using firms (SUFs) criticize that program for causing US sugar prices to be higher than world sugar prices. This study examines the financial performance of publicly traded SUFs to determine if they are performing at an economic disadvantage in terms of accounting profitability, risk and economic profitability compared to other industries.Design/methodology/approachFirm-level financial accounting and market data from 2010 to 2019 were utilized to construct financial metrics for publicly traded SUFs, agribusinesses and general US firms. These financial metrics were analyzed to determine how SUFs compare to their agribusiness peer group and general US companies. The comprehensive financial analysis in this study covers: (1) accounting profit rates, (2) drivers of profitability, (3) economic profit rates, (4) trend analysis and (5) peer comparisons. Quantile regression analysis and Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney statistics are employed for statistical comparisons.FindingsRegarding various profitability and risk measures, SUFs outperform their agribusiness peers and the general benchmark of all US firms in terms of accounting profit rates, risk levels and economic profit rates. Furthermore, compared to other US industries using the 17 French and Fama classifications, SUFs have the highest return on investment and economic profit rate―measured by the Economic Value Added® margin―and the second-lowest opportunity cost of capital, measured by the weighted average cost of capital.Originality/valueThis study finds nothing to suggest that the US sugar program hinders the financial success of SUFs, contrary to recent claims by sugar-using firms. Notably in this analysis is the evaluation of economic profit rates and a series of robustness techniques.

Abstract:
<jats:p>We empirically investigate valuations of Internet firms at various stages of the initial public offering (IPO) from two perspectives. First, we examine the association between the valuation of Internet IPOs and a set of financial and nonfinancial variables, which prior anecdotal or empirical evidence suggests may serve as value drivers. Second, we document differences in IPO valuations between Internet and non‐Internet firms as well as across different stages in the IPO process—i.e., initial prospectus price, final offer price, and first trading day price—within each set of firms. Our primary two conclusions are as follows. First, there are noticeable differences between valuations of Internet and non‐Internet firms, especially at the prospectus and final IPO stage. Specifically, the valuation of non‐Internet firms generally follows the conventional wisdom regarding valuation: positive earnings and cash flows are priced, while negative earnings and negative cash flows are not. The valuation of Internet firms, however, departs from conventional wisdom, with earnings not being priced, and negative cash flows being priced perhaps because they are viewed as investments. This difference between the two classes of firms may be expected, given the age and unique nature of the Internet industry. Second, there are significant differences between the initial valuation of firms at the prospectus and IPO stage and their valuation by the stock market at the end of the first trading day. For non‐Internet firms, the difference is largely ascribed to the relative offering size. For Internet firms, however, the differences are with respect to positive cash flows, sales growth, R&D, and high‐risk warnings, in addition to the relative offering size.</jats:p>

Abstract:
An Initial Public Offering (IPO) is a pivotal moment in a company’s life cycle. It’s a process where a private company offers its shares to the public in the capital market to raise funds. The move from private to public affecting the company to prepare for many changes, including increased supervision and the responsibility of delivering value to shareholders. However, before stepping on this significant IPO step, the company needs a clear understanding of various factors, which includes macroeconomic conditions, the dynamics of the market it operates in, and the company’s internal conditions. The company, PT XYZ, specializes in creating software solutions, a sector that is currently needed by a lot of company due to digitalization era. Fair share price for PT XYZ must be calculated when it goes public. In addition to understanding the macroeconomic condition, the Porter’s Five Forces framework is described to assess the competitive aspect in the market and potential opportunities. After analysing the external factors, the next step is doing in-depth internal analysis. This involved a SWOT analysis by identifying PT XYZ’s Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats, and an evaluation of the company’s financial health. The business solution proceeded to the valuation stage, using the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) method with Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE). This process involved making growth projections for the next decade. It anticipates that the company’s growth rate would eventually align with Indonesia’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP), serving as the long-term growth rate. To ensure a holistic evaluation, there must be a complementary valuation method, Relative Valuation. Three similar companies in the software sector were picked and their EV/EBITDA was used as a multiplier ratio. The two separate valuation methodologies led to two distinct results. Thus the average of these two methods can be proposed. Overvalued or undervalued share pricing can significantly affect investor decisions and the amount of funds raised from the IPO.

Abstract:
For valuation of equity securities and similar objects research has not been rigorous and holistic. This paper is an attempt to review the literature on valuation of equity for a variety of types of entities, and within some important valuation contexts. The review was performed for such themes as (1) Valuation of Stocks (2) Valuation of Private Firms (3) Valuation of Startups (4) Valuation in Emerging Markets (5) Valuation and IPO. The review found that there is a consensus over various models for their usefulness and theoretical soundness, at the same time researchers and practitioner are seeking better models, particularly in the areas of private firm valuation and startups. The valuation of stock has more robust and recognized framework as compared to private firms and startups. The valuation of private firms is more complex because of closed nature of the firm. The valuation of startup is complicated because of the newness of the business and industry, and also because of the nature of the business structure. In general, the practices involving valuation of equity securities and other similar entities have evolved and improved over time. This research will enable the security analysts and other valuation experts to gain insights into various models and their inputs for their beneficial applications.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study explores the implementation of stock valuation approaches, specifically the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) and Multiples Valuation methods (P/E, EV/EBITDA), to determine the intrinsic value of PT XYZ shares in the context of its planned Initial Public Offering (IPO). Although stock valuation is a crucial element in the IPO process, most previous literature focuses on public companies and specific industry sectors, with limited discussion on state-owned construction enterprises (BUMN Karya) within the construction sector. This study contributes theoretically to the stock valuation literature in the construction services sector through a qualitative approach using an exploratory case study on PT XYZ. The DCF analysis is conducted by projecting cash flows using the Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF) approach, discounted by the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), and estimating the share value based on market multiples (P/E and EV/EBITDA). The study also conducts scenario analyses (pessimistic, moderate, optimistic) and sensitivity analyses on key variables such as revenue and cost of goods sold (COGS) to assess the robustness of the valuation under varying assumptions. The results show that the intrinsic value of the shares based on the DCF method ranges from Rp6,627 to Rp28,239 per share, while the multiples valuation yields a range between Rp15,786 and Rp16,868, closely aligning with the moderate DCF scenario result of Rp15,880. These findings highlight the importance of valuation approaches in generating more ideal and realistic share price estimates prior to an IPO. </jats:p>

Abstract:
While traditional organizations create value within the boundaries of their firm or supply chain, digital platforms leverage and orchestrate a platform-mediated ecosystem to create and co-create value with a much wider array of partners and actors. Although the change to two-sided markets and their generalization to platform ecosystems have been adopted among various industries, both academic research and industry adoption have lagged behind in the healthcare industry. To the best of our knowledge current Information Systems research has not yet incorporated an interorganizational perspective of the digital transformation of healthcare. This neglects a wide range of emerging changes, including changing segmentation of industry market participants, changing patient segments, changing patient roles as decision makers, and their interaction in patient care. This study therefore investigates the digital transformation of the healthcare industry by analyzing 1830 healthcare organizations found on Crunchbase. We derived a generic value ecosystem of the digital healthcare industry and validated our findings with industry experts from the traditional and the start-up healthcare domains. The results indicate 8 new roles within healthcare, namely: information platforms, data collection technology, market intermediaries, services for remote and on-demand healthcare, augmented and virtual reality provider, blockchain-based PHR, cloud service provider, and intelligent data analysis for healthcare provider. Our results further illustrate how these roles transform value proposition, value capture, and value delivery in the healthcare industry. We discuss competition between new entrants and incumbents and elaborate how digital health innovations contribute to the changing role of patients.

Abstract:
Entrepreneurship research is on the rise but many questions about its fundamental nature still exist. We argue that entrepreneurship is about experimentation: the probabilities of success are low, extremely skewed and unknowable until an investment is made. At a macro level experimentation by new firms underlies the Schumpeterian notion of creative destruction. However, at a micro level investment and continuation decisions are not always made in a competitive Darwinian contest. Instead, a few investors make decisions that are impacted by incentive, agency and coordination problems, often before a new idea even has a chance to compete in a market. We contend that costs and constraints on the ability to experiment alter the type of organizational form surrounding innovation and influence when innovation is more likely to occur. These factors not only govern how much experimentation is undertaken in the economy, but also the trajectory of experimentation, with potentially very deep economic consequences.

In both periods, technological advances led to not only sharp increases in productivity and dramatic reductions in prices, but also massive obsolescence and overcapacity. And much as the great M&A wave of the 1890s reduced capacity by consolidating some 1,800 companies into roughly 150, the leveraged takeovers, LBOs, and other leveraged recapitalizations of the 1980s provided “healthy adjustments” to overcapacity that was building in many sectors of the U.S. economy. Abstract:
Trial duration is a critical strategic lever for improving subscription conversion rates on Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platforms. While shorter trials in traditional subscription models can effectively boost immediate conversions during the trial period, the Freemium model—where users retain access to basic features after the trial—results in a large population of long-term active free users. Therefore, analyzing conversion in the Freemium context requires attention to both immediate and long-term dynamics. However, systematic empirical research on long-term user conversion under the Freemium model remains limited. This study, conducted in collaboration with a leading global SaaS company, implements a 2-year randomized field experiment involving 680,588 users across 190 countries (2023–2024). We develop a three-stage user conversion model to assess the impact of trial duration on behavior at each stage of the conversion funnel. The results show that extended trial periods significantly increase free trial adoption (Stage 1) and delayed conversion (Stage 3), but have no statistically significant effect on immediate conversion (Stage 2). These findings reflect the interplay between enhanced learning effects and demand cannibalization. Further analyses reveal that users with longer trials respond more favorably to feature-based promotions (e.g., AIGC feature launch), whereas shorter-trial users exhibit greater sensitivity to price-based incentives. Additionally, product functionality and users' economic and cultural contexts moderate the effect of trial duration on conversion. These findings offer practical guidance for optimizing trial design, tailoring promotional strategies, and localizing Freemium-based growth strategies in global SaaS markets.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The freemium business model has become the dominant go-to-market strategy for software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies, yet the majority of firms employing this approach achieve conversion rates of only two to five percent, raising critical questions about optimal freemium design. This case study examines the freemium strategy evolution of CloudMetrics, an anonymized business-to-business SaaS analytics platform that grew from $1.2 million to $14.8 million in annual recurring revenue over a three-year period following its transition from a free-trial model to a freemium offering. Drawing on the theoretical frameworks of network externalities, consumer value theory, and product-led growth, this study traces four distinct phases of CloudMetrics' freemium optimization: an initial feature-gated model, the introduction of usage limits, a hybrid combining both dimensions, and a product-led growth strategy with personalized conversion triggers. The analysis reveals that the hybrid freemium model produced the highest marginal improvement in conversion rates, increasing free-to-paid conversion from 3.8 percent under a feature-only model to 7.4 percent under the fully optimized product-led approach. The case further demonstrates that freemium-acquired customers exhibited 127 percent net revenue retention, substantially exceeding the 109 percent observed among sales-led cohorts. These findings support four research propositions concerning the superiority of hybrid freemium designs, the role of within-organization network effects in amplifying usage-based conversion, the existence of an optimal conversion trigger timing window, and the higher post-conversion quality of freemium-acquired customers. Managerial implications for SaaS practitioners designing and iterating freemium strategies are discussed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Numerous digital services rely on freemium models, yet the mechanisms that move users from free usage to premium subscriptions remain poorly understood. This research examines how expected benefits of premium access, experienced benefits during trials, and habit development in free and premium contexts jointly shape conversion and retention. Across four empirical field studies in a freemium subscription setting, we show that habits in the free version are double‑edged: they can increase conversion by reinforcing expected benefits of the premium version, yet also anchor users in continued free usage through inertia. Habits formed while using the premium version, together with experienced premium benefits, generally support paid conversion and long‑term retention. In discounted trial settings, we further identify an inverse‑U‑shaped relationship between premium‑side habits and retention, with very strong habits associated with lower retention than moderate levels. These insights inform the design of effective freemium and trial strategies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study explores mobile app management and promotion strategies, focusing on how monetization model changes and the use of motivated (incentivized) traffic influence mobile app store visibility, organic growth, and the performance of user acquisition campaigns. The research is grounded on a real-world case of an iOS app “WordFace” developed by the authors, initially distributed for a fixed price and later transitioned to a free-to-download model with in-app subscriptions. The primary objective was to analyze how this shift influences user acquisition cost, conversion rates, and overall return on investment. Methodologically, the study combines practical ads campaigns data with industry benchmarks and digital platforms analytics (SplitMetrics, RevenueCat, Adapty).
Findings show that the switch to a freemium model dramatically reduced the cost per install and increased the conversion rate from impressions to installs. However, the new monetization approach required optimized app onboarding system and subscription funnels to convert free users into paying customers. A structured onboarding process and a 3-day free trial were introduced, increasing trial starts and improving trial-to-paid conversion. Additional experiments compared Apple Search Ads to Facebook Ads, where Facebook proved more cost-effective but required complex attribution tracking. The study also examined motivated installs on the example of KeyApp platform as a tool to boost keyword rankings and organic visibility, yielding mixed results.
The research highlights the trade-offs between volume and user quality in subscription app promotion. While freemium models enhance reach and lower acquisition costs, long-term success hinges on retention and lifetime value (LTV) of acquired users. Future studies may expand the dataset and explore machine learning-based targeting or predictive LTV modeling to further optimize mobile app marketing strategies.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The growth of entrepreneurship and Software as a Service (SaaS) startups in Brazil has increased the challenges of managing recurring revenue models, especially regarding the continuous generation and conversion of leads. This study aimed to develop a comprehensive and measurable model to optimize the growth and sustainability of these companies by integrating strategies for lead generation, nurturing, and commercial and financial management. The research adopted a mixed-method approach, including: (i) exploratory analysis with 15 Brazilian startups to identify key indicators; (ii) inferential analysis of internal metrics from a company; and (iii) Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate the impact of variables on financial performance. The results indicate that smaller companies show low analytical maturity, prioritizing basic metrics, while larger companies adopt more sophisticated indicators and multichannel strategies. Ad Spend and Average Ticket were shown to have the greatest influence on ROI. As contributions, this study offers an applicable model that supports decision-making, increases revenue predictability, and optimizes marketing and sales resources. Limitations include the convenience sampling and the application of the simulation to only one company. It is suggested to expand the sample, conduct longitudinal studies, and apply the model to different SaaS segments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Many popular open source projects are owned and driven by vendors, and in today's difficult economic climate, those vendors are under increasing pressure from investors to deliver a strong return on their investments. One response to this pressure has been the relicensing of popular open source projects to more restrictive licenses in the hopes of generating more revenue, disrupting the idea of open source as a digital commons. In some cases, relicensing has resulted in a hard fork of the original project. These relicensing events and resulting forks can be disruptive to the organizations and individuals using these open source projects. This research compares and contrasts organizational affiliation data from three case studies based on license changes that resulted in forks: Elasticsearch / OpenSearch, Redis / Valkey, and Terraform / OpenTofu. The research indicates that the forks resulting from these relicensing events have more organizational diversity than the original projects, especially when the forks are created under a neutral foundation, like the Linux Foundation, rather than by a single company.

Abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Open source engagement is an ongoing effort in which members continuously interact with evolving project dynamics. Engagement extends beyond writing code or setting policy; it is a shared practice of understanding, negotiating, and adapting to the social and technical structures that define a project. As members continually evaluate their project engagement, collective action threats may arise that impact the overall functioning and sustainability of a project. In our research, we investigate collective action threats and governance practices in relation to a recent trend of vendor defined licence changes that result in project members creating hard forks. Drawing on a netnographic analysis of three cases, Elasticsearch → OpenSearch, Terraform → OpenTofu, and Redis → Valkey, we develop theoretical and practical insights into what collective action threats and governance practices are present, their relationships, and who is involved in them within open source projects that experience relicensing and related hard fork events. Our research provides theoretical and practical implications that show how freeriding accusations become the justification for unilateral, non‐incremental adaptation to a project's boundary regulation and how these governance changes are tied to rebellion as project members reposition themselves within shifting open source landscapes and realign their future open source project engagements.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p> Technology platforms, such as Microsoft Windows, are the hubs of technology industries. We develop a framework to characterize the optimal two-sided pricing strategy of a platform firm; that is, the pricing strategy toward the direct users of the platform as well as toward firms offering applications that are complementary to the platform. We compare industry structures based on a proprietary platform (such as Windows) with those based on an open source platform (such as Linux), and analyze the structure of competition and industry implications in terms of pricing, sales, profitability, and social welfare. We find that, when the platform is proprietary, the equilibrium prices for the platform, the applications, and the platform access fee for applications may be below marginal cost, and we characterize demand conditions that lead to this. The proprietary applications sector of an industry based on an open source platform may be more profitable than the total profits of a proprietary platform industry. When users have a strong preference for application variety, the total profits of the proprietary industry are larger than the total profits of an industry based on an open source platform. The variety of applications is larger when the platform is open source. When a system based on an open source platform with an independent proprietary application competes with a proprietary system, the proprietary system is likely to dominate the open source platform industry both in terms of market share and profitability. This may explain the dominance of Microsoft in the market for PC operating systems. </jats:p>

Abstract:
Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is widely recognized as an important area in cybersecurity but it remains an area showing silos and reserved for large organizations. For an area whose strength is in open and responsive sharing, we see that the generation of feeds has a small scale, is secretive, and is nearly always from specialized businesses that have a commercial interest in not publicly sharing insights at a speed where it could be effective in raising preparedness or stopping an attack. This article has three purposes. First, we extensively review the state and challenges of open, crowd-sourced CTI, with a focus on the perceived barriers. Second, having identified that confidentiality (in multiple forms) is a key barrier, we perform a confidentiality threat analysis of existing sharing architectures and standards, including reviewing circa one million of real-world feeds between 2014 and 2022 from the popular open platform MISP toward quantifying the inherent risks. Our goal is to build the case that, either by redesigning sharing architectures or simply performing simple sanitization of shared information, the confidentiality argument is not as strong as one may have presumed. Third, after identifying key requirements for open crowd-based sharing of CTI, we propose a reference (meta-) architecture. Managerial Relevance—CTI is widely recognized as a key advantage toward cyber resilience in its multiple dimensions, from business continuity to reputation/regulatory protection. Furthermore, as we review in this article, there are strong indications that the next generation of approaches to cybersecurity will be centered on CTI. Whereas CTI is an established business area, we see little adoption, closed communities, or high costs that small businesses cannot afford. For an area that, intuitively, should be open, as velocity and accuracy of information is crucial, we shed light on why we have no significant open, crowd-sourced CTI. In other words, why is usage so lacking? We identify reasons and deconstruct unclear and unhelpful rationales by looking at a wide range of literature (research and professional) and an analysis of nearly ten years of open CTI data. Our findings from current data indicate two types of reasons. One, and dominant, is unhelpful perceptions (e.g., confidentiality), and another stems from market factors (e.g., “free-riding”) that need collective movement as no single player may be able to break the cycle. After looking at motivations and barriers, we review existing technologies, elicit requirements, and propose a high-level open CTI sharing architecture that could be used as a reference for practitioners.

Abstract:
The concept of ‘the commons’ has been used as a framework to understand resources shared by a community rather than a private entity, and it has also inspired social movements working against the enclosure of public goods and resources. One such resource is free (libre) and open source software (FLOSS). FLOSS emerged as an alternative to proprietary software in the 1980s. However, both the products and production processes of FLOSS have become incorporated into capitalist production. For example, Red Hat, Inc. is a large publicly traded company whose business model relies entirely on free software, and IBM, Intel, Cisco, Samsung, Google are some of the largest contributors to Linux, the open-source operating system. This book explores the ways in which FLOSS has been incorporated into digital capitalism. Just as the commons have been used as a motivational frame for radical social movements, it has also served the interests of free-marketeers, corporate libertarians, and states to expand their reach by dragging the shared resources of social life onto digital platforms so they can be integrated into the global capitalist system.  The book concludes by asserting the need for a critical political economic understanding of the commons that foregrounds (digital) labour, class struggle, and uneven power distribution within the digital commons as well as between FLOSS communities and their corporate sponsors.

The tension between open source and proprietary software constitutes one of the
defining structural conflicts of the contemporary digital economy — a conflict that is
simultaneously technical, economic, political, and philosophical. This article presents
a comprehensive comparative and analytical mapping of both paradigms across their
technical, economic, organizational, governance, social, and geopolitical dimensions,
drawing on peer-reviewed scholarship from information systems research, political
economy, organizational theory, science and technology studies, and legal analysis.
The analysis traces the historical emergence of proprietary software as a commercial
category   following   IBM's  1969   unbundling   decision;   the   countervailing
institutionalization of the free software and open source movements from 1983
onward; and the subsequent decades of competitive and collaborative interaction that
have produced the hybrid landscape of the present. Across the technical domains
examined —  operating  systems,  databases,  programming  languages,  cloud
infrastructure, development tooling, artificial intelligence, and cryptographic security
— the article identifies evidence consistent with a structural asymmetry: open source
has achieved categorical dominance at the infrastructure layer of the digital economy,
while proprietary models maintain dominance at the interface and service layers
where economic and political power is concentrated. Key tensions analyzed include
the free rider problem and chronic underinvestment in open source commons; the
strategic commoditization logic by which large technology corporations selectively
open-source  components  to  erode  competitors'  proprietary advantages  while
retaining  proprietary  control  at  value-capturing  layers;  the governance  risks  of
maintainer burnout, corporate capture, and succession failure; the emerging conflicts
between regulatory frameworks — including the EU AI Act, the Cyber Resilience Act,
and data  protection  legislation — and  the open source  ecosystem; and  the
geopolitical dimensions of digital sovereignty in which the open/proprietary choice has
become a matter of national strategic policy. Six paradigmatic case studies — Linux
versus Windows Server, Android's open core architecture, HashiCorp's relicensing of
Terraform,  the Redis and  Elasticsearch  licensing  conflicts  with Amazon Web

1. Introduction

The  history  of  software development has been shaped by a  persistent and
consequential tension between two fundamentally different paradigms: open source
software (OSS), grounded in principles of transparency, collective ownership, and
freedom  of use; and  proprietary  software, characterized by  restricted  access,
centralized control, and commercial licensing. This dichotomy is not merely technical
— it is ideological, economic, and increasingly geopolitical. As digital infrastructure
becomes ever more  central to the functioning  of economies, governments, and
societies, the choice between open and closed software models carries profound
implications for who controls technology, who benefits from  it, and who is excluded
(Bechara & Lechner, 2024; Biström et al., 2024).

A  provocative  starting  point  for  this debate  lies  in a  seemingly  paradoxical
observation: the overwhelming majority of the  digital infrastructure  that runs  the
modern world is built on open source foundations. Linux, the open source operating
system developed by Linus Torvalds in 1991, currently powers approximately 53% of
all servers globally and runs on over 96% of the world's top one million web servers.
All 500  of the world's  fastest supercomputers operate on Linux distributions, a
dominance that has persisted without interruption since 2017. Cloud infrastructure —
the backbone of the digital economy — relies on Linux for more than 90% of its public
workloads. And yet, despite this pervasive adoption, the debate between open source
and proprietary models remains vigorously alive, continuously reinvigorated by shifts
in technology, market structure, and political economy. The question, then, is not

The  roots  of  this  conflict  are found  in the  early 1980s, when the  increasing
commercialization of software prompted Richard Stallman to establish the GNU
Project in 1983 and the Free Software Foundation in 1985, articulating a moral and
political philosophy of software freedom that opposed the emergent proprietary model
(Tolu, 2018). A decade later, Eric S. Raymond's seminal essay "The Cathedral and
the Bazaar" (1997) reframed the argument in engineering and economic terms,
helping to bring the open source movement into mainstream commercial acceptance
and coining the terminological  shift from "free software"  to "open source"  that
occurred in 1998 (Tolu, 2018). Since then, open source development has transitioned
from a countercultural movement into a mainstream industrial practice. Empirical
evidence suggests that the strategic importance of open source to enterprise IT
infrastructure has grown  significantly:  the growing acceptance  of open source
software as a viable part of enterprise information technology infrastructure is an
interesting  contemporary phenomenon  that  continues  to draw  the  attention  of
researchers and practitioners (Esseola et al., 2015). Research from the mid-2010s
onward documents how firms with stronger IT capabilities adopt open source more
broadly,  while  the  heterogeneity  of  software  infrastructure —  combining  both
proprietary and open  source  components —  is  in  fact  the  most common
organizational configuration (Wen & Choudhury, 2019).

The debate, however, has not been resolved by these structural shifts.  If anything,  it
has  intensified  along new  frontiers.  Three  contemporary  developments  have
dramatically re-energized the open source versus proprietary conflict. First, the rapid
expansion of cloud computing has introduced a new form of platform dependency in
which major providers — Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud
— leverage open source software  at  their  infrastructure  layer while  maintaining
proprietary control over services, pricing, and data access, raising novel questions
about vendor lock-in and technological sovereignty (Bechara & Lechner, 2024).

2. Methodological Clarification

This  article  is conceived as a comparative and analytical inquiry rather than an
advocacy document. Its primary objective is to map, systematically and critically, the
key dimensions along which open source software (OSS) and proprietary software
differ, compete, and increasingly converge — without presupposing the superiority of
either model. The  analysis draws on established frameworks from  information
systems  research,  organizational  theory,  political economy, and  science  and
technology studies in order to treat both paradigms as complex social and economic
phenomena  rather  than mere  technical  alternatives  (Fitzgerald, 2006; West &
Gallagher, 2006).

To provide  systematic  structure beyond  narrative  description,  the  comparative
analysis follows a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) logic (Belton & Stewart,

Security and Resilience, (3) Economic Viability and Total Cost of Ownership, (4)
Governance and Transparency, and (5) Sovereignty and Strategic Autonomy. Each
